title: Half steps and whole steps
description: Memorize step sizes, the natural-note map, and the one-fret rule.

cards.back: The distance from one pitch class to the next in the twelve-class chromatic set. The smallest step in ordinary Western music.
Two half steps: skip one pitch class and land on the next.

cards.front: On guitar, how many frets are a half step? A whole step?
cards.back: One fret = one half step. Two frets = one whole step. This holds on any single string, anywhere on the neck.

cards.front: Which two pairs of neighboring naturals are only a half step apart?
cards.back: E to F, and B to C.

cards.front: For each natural pair C–D, D–E, E–F, F–G, G–A, A–B, B–C, is it a whole step or a half step?
cards.back: C–D whole, D–E whole, E–F half, F–G whole, G–A whole, A–B whole, B–C half.

cards.front: Frets get closer toward the body. Does that change the step size?
cards.back: No. Each fret still raises pitch by one half step. The step is a frequency ratio (~5.9%), not a length on the neck.

cards.front: Is counting half steps the same as naming an interval?
cards.back: No. Half steps measure pitch distance. Two different intervals can span the same number of half steps.

cards.front: Are C→C♯ and C→D♭ both one semitone?
cards.back: Yes. Both are one half step, even though they will later have different interval names.

cards.front: Name one half step up from each natural: C D E F G A B.
cards.back: C♯, D♯, F, F♯, G♯, A♯, C. E up and B up land on naturals.

cards.front: Name one half step down from each natural: C D E F G A B.
cards.back: B, C♯, D♯, E, F♯, G♯, A♯. F down and C down land on naturals (E and B).

cards.front: Is G to G♯ a half step even though the letter stays the same?
cards.back: Yes. A half step is a pitch distance, not a letter-name neighbor.

cards.front: From open string 6 (E): what is one fret up? Two frets up?
cards.back: Fret 1 is F (half step). Fret 2 is F♯ (whole step).

cards.front: On string 5, fret 2 is B. What is fret 3? What is fret 5 from fret 3?
cards.back: Fret 3 is C (half step from B). Fret 5 is D (whole step from C).

cards.front: Open string 1 to fret 1 is which step, and why does that match string 6?
cards.back: E to F, a half step — the same relationship as open string 6 to fret 1. Both strings are E strings.

cards.front: Why is “same fret, next string” not a half step?
cards.back: The one-fret rule is for a single string. Adjacent strings are tuned a fourth apart (a major third for G to B), so same-fret neighbors are much larger than a half step.

cards.front: On string 4 (open D), play half step up, then whole step up, then half step up. Name the notes.
cards.back: D♯, then F, then F♯ — each step counted from the previous note.

cards.front: From string 3 open G, move up three whole steps on that string. Fret and note?
Why do scale and chord formulas become usable in any key once steps are solid?
cards.back: They are recipes in whole and half steps from a root. If you can count frets, you can apply the formula instead of memorizing one shape per key.
